scenario.name: NVD, CISA ED 22-02 & GOVCERT.ch — Apache Log4j2 "Log4Shell": JNDI Lookup DFIR & Egress Defense
scenario.shortSubtitle: Network & Web · Log4j2 MessagePatternConverter Lookup Flaw, Zeek LDAP/RMI Egress & Linux auditd execve
scenario.overview: Picture an automated corporate mailroom where a high-speed printing press stamps the return address of every arriving parcel straight into the daily ledger. Because the press mistakenly obeys special pickup orders written on an envelope label instead of treating them as plain ink, a crafted parcel tricks the mailroom into firing a vacuum canister across the street to an unverified annex warehouse to fetch a foreign assembly blueprint, until perimeter guards slam an emerald egress airlock over the outbound tube, catch the mailroom clerk unexpectedly grabbing a workshop wrench, and upgrade the press to print every label strictly as plain text. In this scenario (CVE-2021-44228, Apache Log4j2 Log4Shell JNDI Forensics) targeting APP-JVM-01 through EDGE-GW-02, an untrusted HTTP header crosses from passive log text into active remote code execution along one continuous intrusion path. First, an external probe injects a JNDI lookup header past the edge proxy, then vulnerable log4j-core 2.14.1 evaluates the string through MessagePatternConverter and JndiLookup, then the Java process initiates an abnormal outbound directory callback and spawns a child shell process caught by Zeek and Linux auditd, and finally defenders enforce Log4j 2.17.1+ upgrades and strict egress airlocks. Steps #1 through #4 trace each web, JVM, network, and remediation handoff, while the Memory Forensics section contrasts vulnerable Log4j 2.14.1 lookup evaluation against hardened 2.17.1+ literal logging.

stages.title: Untrusted HTTP Header Enters Logging Pipeline (Nginx & Suricata)
stages.subtitle: Routine Header Logging Exposes Backend Java Service to Lookup Directives
stages.description: An ordinary-looking parcel rolls down the inbound mailroom sorting belt with an unusual bracketed pickup note stamped onto its return label. Even before reaching the main press, the front desk cameras photograph every parcel label so investigators can review who sent it. Almost every production web service logs routine HTTP request fields, such as User-Agent, X-Api-Version, or Referer, for troubleshooting and observability (the standard diagnostic telemetry written to application logs). In CVE-2021-44228, simply logging an untrusted header through vulnerable Log4j2 was enough to trigger lookup evaluation, which is why edge Nginx logs and Suricata SID 2034649 serve as the first forensic checkpoint. When 198.51.100.42 sends an HTTP request to EDGE-GW-02 carrying a JNDI lookup pattern inside X-Api-Version, Nginx preserves the full header in ingress access logs while Suricata SID 2034649 and OWASP CRS rule 944150 raise an immediate warning. Crucially, GOVCERT.ch and CISA noted early in December 2021 that attackers rapidly adopted nested string transformations (like lower/upper case substitutions) to slip past naive static WAF regexes. Consequently, defenders must treat ingress WAF alerts as an early tripwire, never as their sole line of defense. On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ HEADER LOOKUP PROBE / ⇠#1 ALERT HTTP 200) from Node ① (#1 Attacker Exploit & Scanner) to Node ② (#2 DMZ WAF & Reverse Proxy), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Linux Auditd & Elastic SIEM).

stages.title: Log4j2 MessagePatternConverter Evaluates Untrusted Text via JndiLookup
stages.subtitle: Data Becomes Code When Log Messages Trigger Recursive Substitution
stages.description: Inside the cutaway mailroom press, instead of printing the return label as harmless ink, the over-helpful sorting gears recognize the special pickup bracket and treat the outsider’s note as a live internal dispatch command. Log4j2’s MessagePatternConverter (the formatting module that renders log lines before writing them to disk) supported dynamic variable substitution including JndiLookup (Java Naming and Directory Interface, a Java API used to look up directory objects over LDAP, RMI, or DNS). Because log4j2.formatMsgNoLookups defaulted to false in log4j-core 2.0-beta9 through 2.14.1, untrusted data inside a log message silently crossed the boundary from passive text into active network behavior. On APP-JVM-01 (PID 4418), the billing microservice logs the incoming X-Api-Version string using logger.info(). Inside log4j-core-2.14.1.jar, MessagePatternConverter recursively resolves lookup expressions and passes the extracted URI directly to JndiManager and javax.naming.InitialContext.lookup(). A major operational challenge during CISA ED 22-02 response was discovering hidden copies of log4j-core nested inside shaded "fat JARs", WAR files, and third-party vendor appliances, making automated SBOM and filesystem/runtime JAR inventory scanning mandatory. In the documented SBOM / JVM Classpath Audit exchange from DMZ WAF & Reverse Proxy to Java App Server (app-prod-01), Java App Server (app-prod-01) responds with ALERT 2.14.1 (confirming that the JNDILOOKUP EVAL request succeeded on Java App Server (app-prod-01) and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 Outbound Directory Callback & Unexpected Java Child Process (Zeek + auditd)). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ JNDILOOKUP EVAL / ⇠#2 ALERT 2.14.1) from Node ② (#2 DMZ WAF & Reverse Proxy) to Node ③ (#3 Java App Server (app-prod-01)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Linux Auditd & Elastic SIEM).

stages.title: Outbound Directory Callback & Unexpected Java Child Process (Zeek + auditd)
stages.subtitle: Evasion-Resistant Behavioral Detection Beats Header Obfuscation Every Time
stages.description: The mailroom press shoots a glowing canister out through the street-side vacuum tube toward an unverified annex warehouse, and moments later the mailroom clerk unexpectedly picks up a heavy workshop wrench, tripping both the street-tube radar and the internal workshop alarm simultaneously. Regardless of how heavily an attacker obfuscates an inbound HTTP header, exploitation must still cause the Java application server to perform two highly abnormal behaviors: opening an outbound directory connection (TCP/389, 1389, or 1099 caught by Zeek/firewalls) and/or spawning a child OS shell (Linux auditd syscall=59 execve where parent process is java). Both signals are completely immune to HTTP string obfuscation. Production web and billing microservices like APP-JVM-01 (10.20.40.22) have zero legitimate reason to initiate outbound LDAP or RMI connections to external Internet IPs (198.51.100.42:1389) or to fork interactive shell interpreters (/bin/sh, bash, curl, wget) as child processes of PID 4418 (java). Zeek logs the outbound directory handshake and javaNamingReference lookup instantaneously, while Linux auditd records syscall=59 (execve) linking ppid=4418 (java) to pid=5102 (sh). Correlating these two behavioral events delivers rock-solid DFIR proof of active exploitation rather than mere Internet scanning. On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ EGRESS 1389 + JAVA->SH / ⇠#3 ACK PID 5102) from Node ③ (#3 Java App Server (app-prod-01)) to Node ① (#1 Attacker Exploit & Scanner), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Linux Auditd & Elastic SIEM).

stages.title: CISA ED 22-02 Remediation: Log4j 2.17.1+ Upgrade & Strict Egress Airlock
stages.subtitle: Permanent Library Fix Paired With Zero-Trust Outbound Firewall Policy
stages.description: Responding to the dual alarms, facility engineers slam an emerald egress airlock permanently across every outbound street tube, swap the mailroom press core to a literal-ink-only model that ignores bracketed notes forever, and replace any exposed workshop badges. Following CISA Emergency Directive 22-02, durable remediation layers two independent controls: upgrading every Java workload to Apache Log4j 2.17.1 or newer (which completely removes message lookup evaluation and restricts JNDI by default) and enforcing a strict egress firewall airlock (blocking outbound LDAP, LDAPS, and RMI ports from application subnets so future deserialization or lookup flaws cannot call home). Apache’s initial 2.15.0/2.16.0 releases were quickly superseded by Log4j 2.17.1+ (and modern 2.23+ LTS releases), which permanently disable message pattern lookups and harden JNDI configuration. Where active post-exploitation (such as a java->sh execve event) is confirmed, patching in place is not enough: incident responders isolate and re-image APP-JVM-01 from a clean immutable build artifact, rotate all database/cloud/API secrets accessible to appuser, verify no persistent cron jobs or SSH keys remain, and enforce default-deny outbound firewall policies on DMZ application tiers. On the diagram, follow Step #4 / Link #4 (#4→ AIRLOCK + 2.17.1+ FIX / ⇠#4 RESP 2.17.1+) from Node ③ (#3 Java App Server (app-prod-01)) to Node ④ (#4 Java Log4j2 → /bin/bash Shell), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Linux Auditd & Elastic SIEM).

detectionRule.title: Inbound JNDI Lookup Header Pattern (CVE-2021-44228)
detectionRule.ruleCode: alert http $EXTERNAL_NET any -> $HTTP_SERVERS any (msg:"DFIR CVE-2021-44228 Inbound JNDI Lookup Header Pattern"; flow:established,to_server; http.header; content:"jndi"; nocase; pcre:"/\x24\x7b[^\x7d]{0,40}jndi/i"; sid:2034649; rev:3;)

detectionRule.title: Detect Vulnerable log4j-core JndiLookup Class Across Shaded JARs
detectionRule.ruleCode:
rule DFIR_Vulnerable_Log4j2_JndiLookup_Present {
  meta:
    description = "Flags unpatched log4j-core archives bundling JndiLookup prior to 2.17.1"
    cve = "CVE-2021-44228"
  strings:
    $jndi = "org/apache/logging/log4j/core/lookup/JndiLookup.class" ascii
    $ver = "2.14." ascii
  condition:
    $jndi and $ver
}
detectionRule.mitigation: Run continuous SBOM and container/filesystem JAR scans to discover and upgrade every nested log4j-core artifact to >= 2.17.1 (or 2.23+ LTS).

detectionRule.title: Java Application Server Spawning Interactive Unix Shell (auditd execve)
detectionRule.ruleCode:
title: Java Process Spawning Unexpected Shell Interpreter (Log4Shell Post-Exploitation)
status: stable
logsource:
  product: linux
  service: auditd
detection:
  selection:
    type: SYSCALL
    syscall: '59'
    parent_comm: 'java'
    comm:
      - 'sh'
      - 'bash'
      - 'dash'
      - 'curl'
      - 'wget'
  condition: selection
level: critical
detectionRule.mitigation: Alert immediately on outbound LDAP/RMI from web tiers and any java -> shell process spawn; isolate and capture memory before rebuilding.

steps.plainTitle: Outbound Directory Callback & Unexpected Java Child Process (Zeek + auditd)
steps.storyAnalogy: The mailroom press shoots a glowing canister out through the street-side vacuum tube toward an unverified annex warehouse, and moments later the mailroom clerk unexpectedly picks up a heavy workshop wrench, tripping both the street-tube radar and the internal workshop alarm simultaneously.
steps.simpleExplanation: Regardless of how heavily an attacker obfuscates an inbound HTTP header, exploitation must still cause the Java application server to perform two highly abnormal behaviors: opening an outbound directory connection (TCP/389, 1389, or 1099 caught by Zeek/firewalls) and/or spawning a child OS shell (Linux auditd syscall=59 execve where parent process is java). Both signals are completely immune to HTTP string obfuscation.
steps.howItWorksInPractice: Production web and billing microservices like APP-JVM-01 (10.20.40.22) have zero legitimate reason to initiate outbound LDAP or RMI connections to external Internet IPs (198.51.100.42:1389) or to fork interactive shell interpreters (/bin/sh, bash, curl, wget) as child processes of PID 4418 (java). Zeek logs the outbound directory handshake and javaNamingReference lookup instantaneously, while Linux auditd records syscall=59 (execve) linking ppid=4418 (java) to pid=5102 (sh). Correlating these two behavioral events delivers rock-solid DFIR proof of active exploitation rather than mere Internet scanning.
steps.diagramAlignment: Follow Step #3 / Link #3 as Node 3 (APP-JVM-01) attempts an outbound lookup back to Node 1 while Node 4 (Zeek + Linux auditd) flags both the TCP/1389 egress and java->sh execve.
steps.detectionAndEvidence: Alert immediately via Zeek and perimeter firewalls on any outbound TCP/389, 1389, or 1099 connection initiated by web/application tiers, correlated with Linux auditd syscall=59 execve logs showing parent_comm=java spawning sh, bash, curl, or wget.

steps.plainTitle: CISA ED 22-02 Remediation: Log4j 2.17.1+ Upgrade & Strict Egress Airlock
steps.storyAnalogy: Responding to the dual alarms, facility engineers slam an emerald egress airlock permanently across every outbound street tube, swap the mailroom press core to a literal-ink-only model that ignores bracketed notes forever, and replace any exposed workshop badges.
steps.simpleExplanation: Following CISA Emergency Directive 22-02, durable remediation layers two independent controls: upgrading every Java workload to Apache Log4j 2.17.1 or newer (which completely removes message lookup evaluation and restricts JNDI by default) and enforcing a strict egress firewall airlock (blocking outbound LDAP, LDAPS, and RMI ports from application subnets so future deserialization or lookup flaws cannot call home).
steps.howItWorksInPractice: Apache’s initial 2.15.0/2.16.0 releases were quickly superseded by Log4j 2.17.1+ (and modern 2.23+ LTS releases), which permanently disable message pattern lookups and harden JNDI configuration. Where active post-exploitation (such as a java->sh execve event) is confirmed, patching in place is not enough: incident responders isolate and re-image APP-JVM-01 from a clean immutable build artifact, rotate all database/cloud/API secrets accessible to appuser, verify no persistent cron jobs or SSH keys remain, and enforce default-deny outbound firewall policies on DMZ application tiers.
steps.diagramAlignment: Follow Step #4 / Link #4 as Node 5 (Egress Airlock & 2.17.1+) locks down outbound traffic from Node 3 (APP-JVM-01) and verifies clean literal-only logging across the tier.
steps.detectionAndEvidence: Confirm zero log4j-core artifacts below 2.17.1 remain across SBOM scans, verify Zeek and perimeter firewall logs actively deny outbound TCP/389, 636, 1389, and 1099 from application subnets, and monitor SIEM/auditd after rotating exposed service credentials.
